## extender.plugin-incompatible

**Script extender plugin does not support this game version**

- Severity: Error
- Confidence: certain
- Message arguments: `file`, `gameVersion`

The script extender loads native plugins (DLL files) that mods use for features the game cannot provide on its own. Each plugin states which game versions it supports. This one does not support yours, so the script extender refused to load it. The game still starts, but everything the plugin provides is missing, and other mods that rely on it may misbehave.

**What to do:** Look on the mod's page for a version built for your game version and install it. If there is none yet, disable the mod until it has been updated.

## extender.plugin-not-loaded

**Script extender plugin was not loaded**

- Severity: Error
- Confidence: certain
- Message arguments: `file`, `reason`

The script extender tried to load this native plugin (a DLL file) and gave up. The game still starts, but everything the plugin provides is missing. The reason is quoted from the script extender's own log. Common causes are a plugin built for a different game version, a missing requirement such as Address Library, or a damaged download.

**What to do:** Check that the mod's requirements are installed and that the mod matches your game version, then reinstall it. If that does not help, disable the mod and report the quoted reason to its author.

## extender.plugin-no-version-data

**File in the plugin folder is not a script extender plugin**

- Severity: Note
- Confidence: certain
- Message arguments: `file`

Some mods ship support libraries next to their plugin. The script extender examines every DLL in its plugin folder and skips those that carry no plugin information, which is harmless. It only points to a problem if you expected this file to be a plugin: then it is damaged or was built for a different game.

**What to do:** Nothing to do if the file is a support library of one of your mods. If it should be a plugin, reinstall the mod it belongs to.

## plugins.master-missing

**A plugin builds on a plugin that is not installed**

- Severity: Error
- Confidence: certain
- Message arguments: `plugin`, `count`, `masters`

A plugin can build on other plugins, its masters, and names them in its file. The game loads the masters first. If one of them is not there, the game closes without a message while it starts, usually right after the logo. This typically happens when a patch for two mods is installed and one of the two is not, or when a mod was removed and its patches stayed behind.

**What to do:** Install the mod that contains the missing plugin, or disable the mod this plugin belongs to. If the plugin is a patch that an installer offered, run that installer again and untick the patch.

## plugins.generated-outdated

**A generated plugin is older than the load order**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: likely
- Message arguments: `plugin`, `tool`, `count`, `examples`

Some tools look at all your plugins and write a plugin of their own from what they find: DynDOLOD for distant land, Synthesis and Wrye Bash for patches that merge the changes of many mods. Such a plugin is a snapshot. When the load order changes afterwards, because a mod was added, removed or sorted again, the snapshot still holds what was true before. Distant objects may then not match what you see up close, and changes of mods that were sorted again may be lost.

**What to do:** Run the tool that made the plugin again, and replace its old output with the new one. If you keep the output as a mod in your mod manager, install the new output into the same mod.

## plugins.requirement-missing

**A plugin needs a file that is not in the game**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: likely
- Message arguments: `plugin`, `count`, `files`

LOOT, the tool that sorts plugins, keeps a list of what thousands of plugins need and what they do not work with. Mod managers such as Vortex download this list on their own. Many mods only work together with another mod, often a script extender plugin or a library such as PapyrusUtil. Without it, parts of the mod do nothing, its scripts fail, or the game closes as soon as it needs the missing piece.

**What to do:** Install the mod that brings the missing file; the mod's page lists what it needs. If the missing file is a plugin that is installed, switch it on in your mod manager. If you do not want the other mod, disable the mod this plugin belongs to.

## plugins.incompatible

**Two mods do not work together**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: likely
- Message arguments: `plugin`, `other`

Some mods change the same thing in ways that exclude each other: two versions of the same fix, two overhauls of the same part of the game, or an old mod whose work a newer one already contains. LOOT's list names such pairs. With both installed, one undoes the other, features break, or the game becomes unstable.

**What to do:** Decide which of the two you want and disable the other in your mod manager. If one replaces the other, keep the newer one. The mods' pages often say which to choose.

## plugins.needs-cleaning

**A plugin deletes things the game and other mods rely on**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: certain
- Message arguments: `plugin`, `identical`, `deleted`, `navmeshes`, `utility`

Some plugins delete objects of the game outright instead of switching them off, a leftover of how they were made. When another mod or one of the game's scripts refers to a deleted object, the game can crash. Deleted navigation meshes, the paths characters walk on, are the most serious: they can crash the game and cannot be repaired automatically. LOOT's list records which released versions of a plugin contain such deletions. It recognises a version by the file's checksum, so this is about exactly your file.

**What to do:** Install a newer version of the mod if there is one. Otherwise the plugin can be cleaned with SSEEdit's "Quick Auto Clean", which switches deleted objects off instead; LOOT's and SSEEdit's guides explain the steps. Keep a copy of the plugin first. With Vortex, clean the file in the mod's folder in Vortex's staging folder, so that the cleaned file stays. Deleted navigation meshes cannot be cleaned automatically: if there are any, look on the mod's page for a fixed version or a patch.

## plugins.identical-records

**A plugin contains unchanged copies of records**

- Severity: Note
- Confidence: certain
- Message arguments: `plugin`, `count`, `utility`

A record that a plugin copies without changing it does nothing by itself. It matters only when another mod that loads earlier changes the same record: the unchanged copy then quietly puts the original back. That is usually harmless, but it can hide another mod's change. LOOT's list records which released versions of a plugin contain such copies; it recognises a version by the file's checksum.

**What to do:** Usually nothing to do. If a change of another mod does not show in the game, clean this plugin with SSEEdit's "Quick Auto Clean" or let it load before that mod.

## plugins.loot-warning

**LOOT warns about a plugin**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: hint
- Message arguments: `plugin`, `count`, `messages`

LOOT, the tool that sorts plugins, keeps notes about thousands of plugins and shows them when they apply to a setup: a missing compatibility patch, a mod that should not be used together with another, a plugin that should be deleted because another mod already contains it. Mod managers such as Vortex show these notes in their plugin list as well. Mod Mallet quotes them as LOOT writes them, in English, and only those whose conditions hold for your setup.

**What to do:** Read the message and follow it. A missing patch is usually on the page the message names, or offered by the installer of one of the two mods. If the message says to delete or disable a plugin, disable the mod it belongs to in your mod manager.

## plugins.loot-note

**LOOT has a note about a plugin**

- Severity: Note
- Confidence: hint
- Message arguments: `plugin`, `count`, `messages`

LOOT, the tool that sorts plugins, keeps notes about thousands of plugins and shows them when they apply to a setup: an update patch that fixes the mod, a patch collection for it, compatibility notes worth reading, or a hint that the mod needs a new save. Mod Mallet quotes them as LOOT writes them, in English, and only those whose conditions hold for your setup.

**What to do:** Nothing has to be done. Look at the note when you change something about this mod, or when it does not behave as expected.

## npcs.face-mismatch

**Characters with dark or mismatched faces**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: likely
- Message arguments: `count`, `examples`, `winnerPlugin`, `facePlugin`, `faceOrigin`, `faceMod`

The game does not build a character's face while playing. It loads a face mesh that was generated in advance from the character's record. When the record that wins in the load order describes a different face than that mesh was generated from, the game draws the head in the wrong colours, usually much darker than the body. This happens when one mod provides the face files and a plugin of another mod, loaded later, changes the same characters. The check compares the records as written, so it can report a plugin whose change does not show in the game.

**What to do:** If you want the looks of the face files, load their plugin after the other one, or look for a compatibility patch for the two mods. If you want the other plugin's version of the characters, its mod has to provide matching face files.

## installer.options-now-recommended

**Recommended installer options are not installed**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: likely
- Message arguments: `mod`, `count`, `examples`

Many mods come with an installer that offers patches for other mods and ticks the ones that fit what is installed at that moment. The dialog is shown once. If a mod that needs such a patch is installed afterwards, nobody offers the patch again, and the two mods run together unpatched: objects overlap, changes of one mod are lost, or lighting and textures do not match. Mod Mallet replays the installer's own rules against the current setup and reports the options it would tick now. An option you left out on purpose is reported as well.

**What to do:** Reinstall the mod in your mod manager, go through its installer again and tick the options named above. In Vortex, select the mod and choose Reinstall. Deploy and sort the plugins afterwards.

## plugins.contained

**A mod is already part of another**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: likely
- Message arguments: `plugin`, `pluginFile`, `container`, `count`, `total`, `dependentCount`, `dependents`

Collections ("all in one") often contain mods that are also offered on their own. With both installed, their objects stand in the same spot twice: surfaces flicker, and doors and containers can exist twice. Often a patch needs the single mod as a master. Then the single mod cannot simply be switched off: the game would close while starting.

**What to do:** If no other plugin builds on the contained mod, disable it in your mod manager. If a patch builds on it, look on the patch's page for a version made for the collection; many patches come in one version for the single mod and one for the collection. If there is none, keep both and live with the doubled objects for now.

## objects.duplicated

**Two mods place the same object twice**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: likely
- Message arguments: `first`, `second`, `count`, `examples`

Mods that change the same town or the same stretch of land often add the same things, such as a fence, a market stall or a house that the game itself lacks. Each mod places its own copy. The game shows both copies in the same spot, which flickers where the surfaces meet and can make doors or containers appear twice. Mod managers do not show this, because the two mods change different records.

**What to do:** Look on the pages of both mods for a compatibility patch; for well-known combinations there usually is one. Install it with both mods and scan again. If there is none, decide which of the two mods you want to keep for this place, or live with the doubled objects.

## objects.overlapping

**Objects of two mods stand inside each other**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: hint
- Message arguments: `first`, `second`, `count`, `examples`

Two mods that change the same place each put their own buildings, trees or other objects there, without knowing of each other. Where they meet, a tree grows through a roof, two houses merge into one, or a path runs into a wall. Where the models of both objects can be read, Mod Mallet compares their shapes; otherwise only the box around each model, so an object with a lot of empty space, such as an arch, can then be reported although nothing visibly collides.

**What to do:** Look on the pages of both mods for a compatibility patch. If there is none, look at the places named above in the game. If something is in the way, decide which of the two mods you want to keep for this place.

## objects.touching

**Objects of two mods cut into each other**

- Severity: Note
- Confidence: hint
- Message arguments: `first`, `second`, `count`, `examples`

Two mods that place things in the same area did not know of each other, so a fence may run into a wall, a cart may stand half in a market stall, or a lamp post may grow out of a roof. Mod Mallet compared the shapes of both models, not just the boxes around them. Within one mod such contacts are usually wanted, so they are only reported between mods that do not know each other.

**What to do:** Look at the places named above in the game or on the map. Often it does not show; where it does, decide which object you want to keep, or look for a compatibility patch of both mods.

## navmeshes.door-cut-off

**Characters can no longer walk through doors of a mod**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: likely
- Message arguments: `winner`, `loser`, `count`, `places`

The game keeps an invisible net on the ground of every place, which characters use to find their way: its navigation mesh. A door can only be used by characters if the net leads to it. A mod that adds a house connects the net to the house's door. When a later mod replaces the same net with its own version, the door is no longer connected: followers, guards and townspeople stop in front of it or never go in, and quests that send someone through it can get stuck. Only you can still open it.

**What to do:** Look on the pages of both mods for a compatibility patch, and install it if there is one. Without a patch, decide which of the two mods you want to keep for these places. Loading the mod with the door later moves the problem elsewhere: then the other mod's paths are lost.

## navmeshes.changes-undone

**A mod undoes where another mod lets characters walk**

- Severity: Note
- Confidence: likely
- Message arguments: `winner`, `loser`, `count`, `places`

The game keeps an invisible net on the ground of every place, which characters use to find their way: its navigation mesh. A mod that builds a house or a wall changes that net so that people walk around it. A navigation mesh is replaced as a whole, so when two mods change the same one, only the later mod's version counts. People and creatures then walk through the earlier mod's buildings, get stuck at its walls, or no longer find the way into what it added. Followers are often the first to show it.

**What to do:** Look on the pages of both mods for a compatibility patch, and install it if there is one. Without a patch, keep only one of the two mods for these places, or look at them in the game to judge whether it matters there.

## meshes.made-for-other-game

**Meshes of a mod were made for another game**

- Severity: Note
- Confidence: hint
- Message arguments: `count`, `skinned`, `madeFor`, `examples`

A mesh is the 3D shape of a thing in the game. Each game, and each edition of a game, reads meshes in its own variant of the format. Mods for the original Skyrim of 2011 often reached Skyrim Special Edition with some meshes left as they were, and many well-kept mods still ship such meshes. Most of them work. Some do not: then the thing they belong to stays invisible, looks wrong, or the game closes when it appears, most often with clothes, armour and creatures, which bend with a skeleton. This note is a lead for when something like that happens, not a sign that it will.

**What to do:** Nothing to do while the game runs well. If something of this mod crashes the game or stays invisible, look on the mod's page for a version made for your game and install that instead. If there is none, the meshes can be converted with Cathedral Assets Optimizer, a free tool made for exactly this; then install the converted files as a mod of their own that overwrites this one.

## meshes.texture-missing

**Meshes of a mod use textures that are not in the game**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: hint
- Message arguments: `meshes`, `count`, `examples`

A mesh is the 3D shape of a thing; its colour and the fine detail of its surface come from textures, separate image files that the mesh names. If a named texture is not there, the game draws the surface in a glaring purple, or dark and flat where the surface detail is missing. This usually means that a part of the mod was not installed, for example its textures in a separate download, or that the mod was made to go with another mod you do not have. Meshes a mod installs for a mod you do not use are never shown, so their missing textures do no harm.

**What to do:** Look on the mod's page for files that belong with it, such as a texture download or a mod it needs, and install them. If the meshes are part of a patch for a mod you do not have, you can leave them.

## meshes.retexture-bypassed

**A texture mod does not reach replaced meshes**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: likely
- Message arguments: `count`, `examples`, `meshOrigin`, `meshMod`, `textureMod`

A mesh names the textures it uses by path. A texture mod works by providing new files under the paths the original meshes name. When another mod replaces a mesh and its version names other paths, usually textures in that mod's own folder, the texture mod no longer reaches the object. The object keeps one look while everything around it gets the new one: a bright wall next to dark ones, a sharp roof next to blurry ones. How much it shows depends on how different the two sets of textures are.

**What to do:** Check whether the texture mod offers an option or a patch for the mesh mod; many do. Otherwise decide which look you prefer: remove the listed meshes of the mesh mod, so that the original meshes and the texture mod apply, or keep them and accept the difference.

## assets.loose-over-archive

**Loose files cover files in another mod's archive**

- Severity: Note
- Confidence: certain
- Message arguments: `count`, `examples`, `winnerOrigin`, `winnerMod`, `archive`, `archiveMod`

A mod can ship its files packed into an archive or as loose files. The game always prefers a loose file over the same file in an archive, whatever the order of the mods. Mod managers show conflicts between loose files but not this kind, because one side is hidden inside the archive. Often it is intended, for example a texture pack over an older mod. It becomes a problem when only some of the files that belong together are replaced, such as a mesh without its texture: the result can be purple or misplaced objects.

**What to do:** Nothing to do if you want the loose files to win. If the mod in the archive looks broken in the game, disable the mod that provides the loose files, or check on its page whether the two are compatible.

## assets.archive-over-archive

**An archive covers files in another mod's archive**

- Severity: Note
- Confidence: certain
- Message arguments: `count`, `examples`, `winnerArchive`, `winnerOrigin`, `winnerMod`, `archive`, `archiveMod`

Archives are loaded in the order of the plugins they belong to. When two archives contain the same file, the game uses the one loaded later. Mod managers do not show this, because both sides are hidden inside archives. It is harmless when the later mod is meant to build on the earlier one. It is a problem when the later archive carries older copies of files that it shares with the earlier mod.

**What to do:** Nothing to do if the later mod is meant to win. Otherwise change the load order of the two plugins so that the archive you want is loaded last.

## setup.file-unreadable

**A file of the setup could not be read**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: certain
- Message arguments: `file`, `reason`

Mod Mallet skipped this file, so problems that involve it are not reported. If the file is damaged, the game may have trouble with it as well. A damaged download is the usual cause.

**What to do:** Reinstall the mod the file belongs to. If the game works with the file and Mod Mallet does not, please report it.

## crashes.in-dll

**The game crashed inside a mod's program file**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: likely
- Message arguments: `file`, `count`, `last`

Some mods bring a program file of their own, a DLL that the script extender loads into the game. When the game crashes while running that file's code, the file is the most likely cause: it may not fit the game's version, clash with another such file, or have a bug. It is not certain: the file may also have been handed broken data by something else.

**What to do:** Look on the mod's page for an update and for known problems with your game version. If the crashes go on, disable the mod for a while and see whether they stop.

## crashes.mod-involved

**Recent crash reports point at a mod**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: hint
- Message arguments: `count`, `last`, `examples`

Crash reports list what was in use when the game failed: characters, objects, meshes, and program files on the way to the crash. When things of one mod turn up there, the mod may be involved, for example through a broken mesh or a character with an odd setup. It may also just have been close by, especially when the crash happened in a busy place. The more reports point at the same mod, the more likely it is involved.

**What to do:** If several reports point at this mod, look on its page for known crashes and patches. To be sure, disable it for a while, or avoid the place or thing named above, and see whether the crashes stop.

## crashes.recent

**The game crashed recently**

- Severity: Note
- Confidence: certain
- Message arguments: `count`, `days`, `last`, `examples`

A crash logger is a small addition to the script extender that writes a report every time the game crashes. The report says in which program file the game failed and lists what was nearby: characters, objects, meshes and the mods they come from. Reading it is a matter of likelihood, not certainty. Mod Mallet looks at the reports of the last weeks and says which mods they point at; a crash inside the game itself with nothing of a mod nearby is counted but not blamed on anyone.

**What to do:** Look at the other findings about crashes, if there are any. If the game crashes at one place again and again, note what you were doing; that helps whoever looks into it.

## setup.load-order-unknown

**The load order could not be read**

- Severity: Warning
- Confidence: certain
- Message arguments: `reason`

Mod Mallet needs to know which plugins are active and in which order the game loads them. Without that it cannot tell which files and records win, so those checks did not run. The other checks are not affected.

**What to do:** Start the game or your mod manager once so that the list of plugins is written, then scan again. If the game is installed in an unusual place, tell Mod Mallet where it is.

## mods.collides-widely

**Suggestion: a mod collides with many places of other mods**

- Severity: Note
- Confidence: hint
- Message arguments: `mod`, `count`, `modCount`, `others`, `objects`, `total`

This is only a suggestion; nothing is broken. Two mods that change the same part of the world without knowing of each other put their buildings, trees and fences where the other already has something. A few such places are normal and are listed one by one under collisions. When one mod collides this often, it and the other mods were probably not made to be used together.

**What to do:** Decide which version of these places you prefer. If it is the other mods', you can switch the mod off in your mod manager, or keep it and, in the list of collisions, let it lose against the other mods in every place at once. If you like the mod, keep it, and look on its page for a patch that makes it work with the other mods.

## mods.mostly-overridden

**Suggestion: hardly anything of a mod reaches the game**

- Severity: Note
- Confidence: hint
- Message arguments: `mod`, `total`, `surviving`, `percent`, `overriders`

This is only a suggestion; nothing is broken. When two mods change the same thing, the game uses the version of the mod it loads later. Mod Mallet compared the objects the mod places, the characters it changes, and the files in its archives. A mod can bring other things as well, such as quests, items or scripts, which are not counted here.

**What to do:** If you do not miss anything from the mod in the game, you can switch it off in your mod manager; that makes the setup simpler and loads faster. Before you do, check its page: some mods are needed by others, and those would then stop working. If you prefer the version of the mod, place its plugin after the mods named above.

## mods.duplicates-another

**Suggestion: a mod places largely the same objects as another**

- Severity: Note
- Confidence: hint
- Message arguments: `mod`, `other`, `count`, `total`, `patchCount`, `patches`, `otherPatchCount`, `otherPatches`

This is only a suggestion; nothing is broken. Collections ("all in one") often contain mods that are also offered on their own, and two mods can rebuild the same place in the same way. With both installed, the same buildings stand twice in the same spot and their surfaces flicker. A plugin made for one of the two, such as a compatibility patch, only works with that one, which is a good reason to keep it.

**What to do:** Keep the one you prefer and switch the other off in your mod manager; prefer the one the patches you use are made for. Before you switch one off, check whether it brings something the other lacks, such as an interior: then keep both, and in the list of collisions let one of them lose in every place at once.
